questions.stem:
A 52-year-old woman with a penicillin allergy has community-acquired pneumonia with lobar consolidation. Sputum Gram stain shows lancet-shaped Gram-positive diplococci. Her physician wants an oral fluoroquinolone that reliably covers this organism and atypical pathogens, and that can also be used if she later develops a urinary tract infection.

Which fluoroquinolone fits best?
choices: Levofloxacin, a respiratory agent with good streptococcal coverage
Ciprofloxacin, because it has the strongest Gram-negative activity of the class
Moxifloxacin, because it has the greatest anaerobic activity of the class
Ciprofloxacin, because poor urinary levels are not a concern in pneumonia
Moxifloxacin, because it is renally excreted and reaches high urine levels

explain.html:
Lancet-shaped Gram-positive diplococci are Streptococcus pneumoniae. The lecture divides the class: ciprofloxacin has poor streptococcal coverage and is not indicated for community-acquired pneumonia; levofloxacin and moxifloxacin are the "respiratory fluoroquinolones," active against S. pneumoniae and atypicals.

Between the two respiratory agents, moxifloxacin is metabolized by the liver and does not reach adequate urinary concentrations, so it cannot treat a urinary tract infection. Levofloxacin covers S. pneumoniae, atypicals and some Pseudomonas, and is renally excreted, so it fits both needs.
why: Ciprofloxacin has poor streptococcal coverage and is not used for community-acquired pneumonia.
Moxifloxacin covers pneumonia but cannot be used for urinary tract infections.
Ciprofloxacin fails the pneumonia indication because of poor S. pneumoniae activity.
Moxifloxacin is the fluoroquinolone that is not renally excreted and has poor urinary levels.
explain.takeaway: Levofloxacin and moxifloxacin are respiratory fluoroquinolones active against S. pneumoniae; ciprofloxacin is not used for pneumonia, and moxifloxacin is not used for UTIs.
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 70-year-old man has Enterococcus faecalis endocarditis. Given alone in the laboratory, gentamicin barely affects the isolate, and ampicillin alone only slows its growth. When the two are combined, the culture is killed rapidly. The same gentamicin dose readily kills Pseudomonas aeruginosa without any partner drug.

Which explanation best accounts for the rapid killing with the combination?
choices: Gentamicin inhibits the beta-lactamase that degrades ampicillin in enterococci
Ampicillin damage to the cell wall increases gentamicin entry to the 30S ribosomal subunit
Ampicillin and gentamicin bind two different sites on the 50S subunit together
Gentamicin blocks efflux pumps that would otherwise remove ampicillin
The combination blocks two sequential steps in bacterial folate synthesis

explain.html:
Aminoglycosides irreversibly bind the 30S ribosomal subunit, cause misreading of messenger RNA and are bactericidal. Used alone they have only Gram-negative activity, including Pseudomonas. Against Gram-positive organisms such as Enterococcus and S. aureus, they are used for synergy with a cell wall agent.

The lecture's explanation is that beta-lactams or vancomycin weaken the cell wall and increase aminoglycoside entry into the bacterium, letting the drug reach its ribosomal target. That is why ampicillin plus gentamicin is a classic regimen for enterococcal endocarditis.
why: The mechanism is enhanced uptake, not inhibition of a beta-lactamase.
Aminoglycosides bind the 30S subunit, and ampicillin does not bind ribosomes.
Aminoglycosides do not inhibit efflux pumps.
Sequential folate blockade describes trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.
explain.takeaway: Aminoglycosides alone cover Gram-negatives (including Pseudomonas); against Gram-positives they act synergistically with cell wall inhibitors, which increase their entry.
explain.topic: Aminoglycoside synergy with cell wall agents
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 30-year-old woman who is 14 weeks pregnant has a cough and is diagnosed with atypical pneumonia. A clinician considers a drug that reversibly binds the 30S ribosomal subunit and blocks aminoacyl-tRNA from attaching to the A site. A colleague advises against it in this patient.

Which adverse effect is the main reason to avoid this drug class in pregnancy?
choices: Irreversible ototoxicity of the developing inner ear
Neural tube defects from folate antagonism
Neonatal jaundice from displacement of bilirubin
Interstitial nephritis of the fetal kidney
Staining and deformity of developing teeth

explain.html:
Reversible 30S binding that blocks aminoacyl-tRNA attachment at the A site is the tetracycline mechanism, which halts elongation and is bacteriostatic. Tetracyclines would cover atypical pneumonia, which is why the drug was considered.

The lecture's tetracycline adverse effects are hepatotoxicity, chelation of cations, photosensitivity, esophagitis, and staining or deformity of teeth, with a clear warning to avoid them in pregnancy. Developing teeth (and bone) bind the drug, which is why tetracyclines are avoided in pregnancy and young children.
why: Ototoxicity is the aminoglycoside concern.
Folate antagonism belongs to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, not tetracyclines.
Neonatal jaundice from the drug is the ceftriaxone concern taught in this block.
Interstitial nephritis is linked to nafcillin, not tetracyclines.
explain.takeaway: Tetracyclines bind 30S reversibly to block tRNA at the A site; they stain and deform developing teeth and are avoided in pregnancy.
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 61-year-old man in a long-term care facility has a wound infection with several resistant organisms. The lab reports MRSA, vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus (VRE), an ESBL-producing Klebsiella, and a fourth isolate. The team chooses a glycylcycline because it covers resistant Gram-positives, ESBL producers and anaerobes, but a pharmacist warns that one isolate will not be covered.

Which fourth isolate would this drug miss?
choices: Acinetobacter baumannii
Bacteroides fragilis
Proteus mirabilis
Streptococcus pyogenes
Escherichia coli

explain.html:
Tigecycline (and eravacycline) extend the tetracycline spectrum to ESBL-producing Gram-negatives, Acinetobacter, MRSA, VRE, anaerobes and some mycobacteria. The lecture marks its gaps as the "4 Ps": no Pseudomonas, no Proteus, no Providencia, no Morganella (formerly Proteus).

So in this mixed infection, Proteus mirabilis is the organism the drug would leave uncovered.
why: Tigecycline covers Acinetobacter, including resistant strains.
Tigecycline has anaerobic activity, including Bacteroides.
Tigecycline covers Gram-positive cocci, including resistant ones.
Tigecycline covers Gram-negatives such as E. coli, including ESBL producers.
explain.takeaway: Tigecycline and eravacycline cover MRSA, VRE, ESBL producers, Acinetobacter and anaerobes but not the "4 Ps": Pseudomonas, Proteus, Providencia, Morganella.
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 38-year-old man with a deep neck abscess from an infected molar is treated with an oral drug that binds the 50S subunit, inhibits peptidyl transferase and is chosen because it covers Gram-positive cocci including MRSA as well as oral anaerobes. Ten days later he has 8 watery stools daily, crampy abdominal pain and a white blood cell count of 18,000/microL (normal 4,500 to 11,000). Colonoscopy shows yellow-white plaques on the colonic mucosa.

Which statement about the antibiotic he received is correct?
choices: It is intrinsically active against most Gram-negative rods
It is the oral drug of choice for this patient's colitis
It acts at the 30S subunit and is bactericidal against all MRSA
It shows no cross-resistance with macrolide antibiotics
It covers anaerobes and toxin makers but not Gram-negatives

explain.html:
A 50S binder that inhibits peptidyl transferase, covers MRSA and anaerobes and is used for oropharyngeal and skin infections is clindamycin, a lincosamide. It is bacteriostatic. The lecture lists its spectrum as Gram-positives including MRSA, anaerobes and an anti-toxin effect against toxin-producing Gram-positive organisms, with no Gram-negative activity (intrinsic resistance) and lots of resistance, including cross-resistance with macrolides.

His diarrhea with pseudomembranes is C. difficile colitis, the adverse effect the lecture ties most closely to clindamycin. Clindamycin causes it; it does not treat it (oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin do).
why: Gram-negatives are intrinsically resistant to clindamycin.
Clindamycin causes pseudomembranous colitis; it is not a treatment for it.
Clindamycin binds the 50S subunit and is bacteriostatic.
There is cross-resistance between clindamycin and macrolides.
explain.takeaway: Clindamycin (50S, peptidyl transferase, bacteriostatic) covers Gram-positives including MRSA, anaerobes and toxin producers, has no Gram-negative activity, and is strongly linked to C. difficile colitis.
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 55-year-old man with peptic ulcer disease from Helicobacter pylori is started on triple therapy that includes a macrolide. He also takes a drug for which small increases in blood level cause toxicity. Two days later his level of that drug has nearly doubled. His physician notes that switching to azithromycin would likely have avoided this interaction, though azithromycin is not the agent used in triple therapy.

Which macrolide was most likely prescribed, and what explains the interaction?
choices: Azithromycin, by chelating the drug in the gut
Clarithromycin, by inhibiting hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes
Erythromycin, by speeding gastric emptying
Clarithromycin, by blocking renal tubular secretion
Fidaxomicin, by binding bacterial RNA polymerase

explain.html:
Macrolides bind the 50S subunit, block translocation of the peptide chain from the A site to the P site and are bacteriostatic. The lecture lists clarithromycin as the macrolide used in H. pylori triple therapy.

The protein synthesis inhibitor table flags CYP inhibition, especially with erythromycin and clarithromycin, which raises levels of other drugs metabolized by those enzymes. Azithromycin has much less of this effect. Erythromycin's prokinetic action is a separate feature (it is used for GI motility) and would not double a drug level.
why: Azithromycin is not the triple therapy macrolide, and chelation is a tetracycline problem.
Erythromycin speeds GI motility, but it is not the triple therapy agent and motility does not explain the level.
The interaction is hepatic CYP inhibition, not renal secretion.
Fidaxomicin is used only for C. difficile.
explain.takeaway: Macrolides bind 50S and block translocation; clarithromycin is part of H. pylori triple therapy, and erythromycin and clarithromycin inhibit CYP enzymes, raising other drug levels.
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 72-year-old woman has her third episode of Clostridioides difficile colitis in 4 months. Each prior episode responded to treatment but returned. Her physician chooses a macrocyclic agent that is used exclusively for this infection and is more effective at preventing recurrence. Unlike other drugs in its broad structural family, it does not act on the ribosome.

Which step does this drug block?
choices: Translocation of the growing peptide chain on the 50S subunit
Reduction of a nitro group to toxic free radicals in anaerobes
Formation of the 70S initiation complex at the 23S rRNA
Supercoiling of DNA by DNA gyrase during replication
Opening and closing of the RNA polymerase clamp at transcription initiation

explain.html:
The drug is fidaxomicin, a macrocyclic macrolide used only for C. difficile infection and more effective than alternatives at preventing recurrence. Its target is bacterial RNA polymerase: it binds the switch region and prevents the enzyme from opening and closing the DNA clamp, blocking transcription initiation and mRNA synthesis.

That sets it apart from the classic macrolides, which bind the 50S ribosomal subunit and block translocation. Its main adverse effect is GI disturbance.
why: Blocking translocation on the 50S subunit is how azithromycin and other classic macrolides act.
Nitro group reduction to free radicals is the metronidazole mechanism.
Blocking the 70S initiation complex at 23S rRNA is linezolid.
DNA gyrase is the fluoroquinolone target.
explain.takeaway: Fidaxomicin binds bacterial RNA polymerase to block transcription initiation, is used only for C. difficile, and better prevents recurrence.
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
In a laboratory study of Escherichia coli, drug X alone blocks formation of dihydrofolic acid and only slows growth. Drug Y alone blocks the conversion of dihydrofolic acid to tetrahydrofolic acid and also only slows growth. Given together, the two drugs kill the bacteria. Human cells are much less affected because they take up preformed folate rather than synthesizing it.

Which pair of enzymes do drugs X and Y inhibit, in order?
choices: DNA gyrase, then topoisomerase IV
Dihydrofolate reductase, then dihydropteroate synthase
Dihydropteroate synthase, then dihydrofolate reductase
Peptidyl transferase, then RNA polymerase
Thymidylate synthase, then dihydropteroate synthase

explain.html:
This is trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Sulfamethoxazole (drug X) inhibits dihydropteroate synthase and blocks formation of dihydrofolic acid. Trimethoprim (drug Y) inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, the later step that converts dihydrofolic acid to tetrahydrofolic acid.

Blocking two sequential steps of folate synthesis starves the cell of the folate needed for DNA synthesis. The lecture notes the synergy: each drug alone is weaker, but the combination is bactericidal.
why: DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV are fluoroquinolone targets.
This reverses the order; dihydropteroate synthase acts first, and that is the sulfonamide target.
Peptidyl transferase and RNA polymerase are targets of clindamycin and fidaxomicin.
Thymidylate synthase is not a target taught for these drugs.
explain.takeaway: Sulfamethoxazole inhibits dihydropteroate synthase and trimethoprim inhibits dihydrofolate reductase; sequential folate blockade makes the combination bactericidal.
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 74-year-old man on long-term oral prednisone for polymyalgia rheumatica is treated for a complicated urinary tract infection with an oral drug that has excellent bioavailability (oral nearly equal to intravenous) and strong Gram-negative and Pseudomonas activity but poor streptococcal coverage. On day 5, while stepping off a curb, he feels a sudden pop at the back of his right ankle and cannot rise onto his toes.

The drug that caused this injury kills bacteria by inhibiting which target?
choices: The 30S ribosomal subunit, causing misreading of messenger RNA
DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, blocking DNA replication
Dihydrofolate reductase, blocking the last step of folate synthesis
Penicillin-binding proteins, blocking peptidoglycan cross-linking
Bacterial RNA polymerase, blocking the start of transcription

explain.html:
An oral agent with oral bioavailability close to intravenous, strong Gram-negative and Pseudomonas coverage, poor streptococcal coverage and a role in urinary infections is ciprofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone. The sudden pop and loss of plantar flexion describe Achilles tendon rupture, a fluoroquinolone adverse effect that the lecture flags especially in the elderly and in patients taking corticosteroids.

Fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II, mainly in Gram-negatives) and topoisomerase IV (mainly in Gram-positives), blocking DNA replication and repair. Their killing is concentration dependent and bactericidal.
why: 30S binding with misreading is the aminoglycoside mechanism; aminoglycosides cause ototoxicity, not tendon rupture.
Dihydrofolate reductase is the trimethoprim target.
PBP binding is the beta-lactam mechanism.
RNA polymerase is the target of fidaxomicin.
explain.takeaway: Fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV; tendinopathy and tendon rupture are a key adverse effect, especially in older patients on corticosteroids.
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 63-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation who takes an antiarrhythmic drug is started on levofloxacin for pneumonia. On day 2 an outpatient physician, unaware of the first prescription, adds a second antibiotic that binds the 50S ribosomal subunit and blocks translocation, to cover Mycoplasma. That evening she faints, and telemetry shows a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with twisting QRS complexes.

Which shared effect of the two antibiotics best explains this event?
choices: Hyperkalemia from blockade of sodium channels in the distal nephron
Direct histamine release that causes vasodilation and hypotension
Serotonin excess from weak inhibition of monoamine oxidase
Delayed cardiac repolarization that prolongs the QT interval
Neuromuscular blockade that weakens the respiratory muscles

explain.html:
The second drug, a 50S binder that blocks translocation and covers Mycoplasma, is a macrolide (such as azithromycin). Both fluoroquinolones and macrolides prolong the QTc interval by inhibiting cardiac repolarization, and the lecture notes QT prolongation with fluoroquinolones especially in combination with macrolides, with caution and closer monitoring when antiarrhythmics are also given.

Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with twisting complexes is torsades de pointes, the arrhythmia the lecture lists under fluoroquinolone cardiac toxicity. Stacking two QT-prolonging antibiotics on an antiarrhythmic is the setup.
why: Hyperkalemia is a trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole effect, and neither drug here causes it.
Rate-related histamine release is vancomycin flushing syndrome.
Weak MAO inhibition with serotonin syndrome is a linezolid effect.
Neuromuscular blockade is an aminoglycoside effect.
explain.takeaway: Fluoroquinolones and macrolides both prolong the QT interval; combining them, especially with antiarrhythmics, risks torsades de pointes.
explain.topic: QT prolongation with fluoroquinolones and macrolides
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 66-year-old woman with myasthenia gravis and chronic kidney disease is treated for Pseudomonas bacteremia with a bactericidal drug that binds the 30S ribosomal subunit irreversibly and has a narrow therapeutic window requiring drug-level monitoring. Over the course of therapy the team worries about several toxicities.

Which set of adverse effects should the team monitor most closely with this drug?
choices: Tendon rupture, QT prolongation and photosensitivity
Tooth staining, esophagitis and hepatotoxicity
Thrombocytopenia, optic neuritis and lactic acidosis
Ototoxicity, nephrotoxicity and neuromuscular blockade
Creatine kinase elevation, myopathy and eosinophilic pneumonia

explain.html:
Irreversible 30S binding, bactericidal activity and a narrow therapeutic window that requires levels describe an aminoglycoside (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin). The class-wide adverse effects in the lecture are ototoxicity (auditory and vestibular, possibly irreversible), nephrotoxicity as acute tubular necrosis, and neuromuscular blockade.

Her history makes each one worse: chronic kidney disease raises nephrotoxicity risk, and myasthenia gravis raises the risk of flaccid paralysis or respiratory depression from neuromuscular blockade.
why: Tendon rupture, QT prolongation and photosensitivity are fluoroquinolone effects.
Tooth staining, esophagitis and hepatotoxicity are tetracycline effects.
Thrombocytopenia, optic neuritis and lactic acidosis are linezolid effects.
Creatine kinase elevation, myopathy and eosinophilic pneumonia are daptomycin effects.
explain.takeaway: Aminoglycoside class toxicities are ototoxicity, nephrotoxicity (acute tubular necrosis) and neuromuscular blockade, worse in kidney disease and myasthenia gravis.
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 28-year-old man returns from camping in North Carolina with fever, headache and a petechial rash that began on the wrists and ankles and spread to the trunk, including the palms. He recalls removing a tick. He is started on the drug of choice for this infection. He usually takes it with his morning glass of milk and an over-the-counter antacid for heartburn.

What is the main concern with how he is taking the drug?
choices: Divalent cations in milk and antacids chelate it in the gut
Milk and antacids speed its renal clearance and require a higher dose
Antacids raise gastric pH and convert the drug to a toxic metabolite
Calcium in milk precipitates the drug in the bile and causes sludging
Milk proteins bind the drug in plasma and prevent it from entering cells

explain.html:
Fever, headache and a petechial rash moving from wrists and ankles to the trunk after a tick bite describes Rocky Mountain spotted fever, a rickettsial disease. The lecture names doxycycline the drug of choice for most infections caused by rickettsiae and Borrelia, because tetracyclines penetrate cells and kill intracellular pathogens.

Tetracyclines chelate divalent cations, so milk, antacids and iron supplements bind the drug in the gut and reduce absorption. He should separate doses from these products.
why: Tetracyclines are mostly cleared by the liver; the interaction is in the gut, not the kidney.
Raised gastric pH does not create a toxic metabolite of doxycycline.
Calcium precipitation and biliary sludging are ceftriaxone problems.
The interaction is chelation in the gut, not plasma protein binding.
explain.takeaway: Doxycycline is the drug of choice for rickettsial infections and Lyme disease; tetracyclines chelate divalent cations (milk, antacids, iron), which blocks absorption.
explain.topic: Doxycycline for rickettsial disease and chelation
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 47-year-old woman with depression treated with sertraline is admitted with a complicated skin infection caused by vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium. She is started on a bacteriostatic drug that binds the 23S rRNA of the 50S subunit and prevents formation of the 70S initiation complex. Two days later she is agitated and diaphoretic, with a temperature of 38.8 C (101.8 F), heart rate 124/min, tremor, hyperreflexia and inducible clonus.

Which property of the antibiotic best explains her new findings?
choices: It has weak monoamine oxidase inhibitor activity
It inhibits hepatic cytochrome enzymes and raises sertraline levels
It prolongs cardiac repolarization and causes sympathetic surge
It suppresses the marrow and causes fever from neutropenia
It causes lactic acidosis that stimulates the nervous system

explain.html:
Binding the 23S rRNA of the 50S subunit to block the 70S initiation complex is the linezolid (oxazolidinone) mechanism. Linezolid covers MRSA, VRE and penicillin-resistant S. pneumoniae.

Agitation, fever, tachycardia, tremor, hyperreflexia and clonus in a patient taking an SSRI are serotonin syndrome. The lecture warns that linezolid causes serotonin syndrome when combined with other serotonergic agents because of its weak monoamine oxidase inhibitor activity. Its other adverse effects are thrombocytopenia after about 2 weeks, peripheral and optic neuropathy and, rarely, lactic acidosis.
why: CYP inhibition is the macrolide (erythromycin, clarithromycin) interaction, not linezolid's.
QT prolongation is a fluoroquinolone and macrolide effect and does not produce clonus.
Linezolid myelosuppression is mainly thrombocytopenia after about 2 weeks, not this neuromuscular picture.
Lactic acidosis is a rare linezolid effect but does not explain clonus and hyperreflexia.
explain.takeaway: Linezolid binds 23S rRNA of the 50S subunit to block initiation, covers MRSA and VRE, and causes serotonin syndrome with serotonergic drugs (weak MAOI), plus thrombocytopenia after about 2 weeks.
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 41-year-old man with advanced HIV infection and a CD4 count of 60/microL has progressive dyspnea and a dry cough. Bronchoalveolar lavage shows cysts of a fungal organism on silver stain. He is started on the antibiotic combination the lecture lists for this pneumonia. On day 5 his labs are drawn.

Sodium: 136 mEq/L (135 to 145)
Potassium: 6.2 mEq/L (3.5 to 5.0)
Creatinine: 1.3 mg/dL (0.6 to 1.2)

The abnormal potassium is a known effect of this drug, which also covers which organism?
choices: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Bacteroides fragilis
Nocardia species
Enterococcus faecium
Mycoplasma pneumoniae

explain.html:
Silver-staining cysts in an HIV patient with a low CD4 count point to Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP), and the lecture lists trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for PCP. Hyperkalemia is one of its listed adverse effects, along with crystalluria, marrow suppression, photosensitivity, rash and Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

Its spectrum in the lecture includes Gram-positives including MRSA, Gram-negatives such as E. coli, Klebsiella and Stenotrophomonas (but no Pseudomonas), and others: Pneumocystis, Nocardia and Listeria.
why: TMP-SMX has no Pseudomonas activity.
Anaerobes such as B. fragilis are not part of its spectrum; metronidazole covers them.
VRE is not covered by TMP-SMX.
Atypicals such as Mycoplasma are covered by macrolides, tetracyclines and respiratory fluoroquinolones.
explain.takeaway: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole treats PCP and covers MRSA, Nocardia, Listeria and Stenotrophomonas (not Pseudomonas); hyperkalemia is a key adverse effect.
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 33-year-old woman has a frothy, malodorous vaginal discharge, and a wet mount shows motile flagellated protozoa. She is treated with a drug that is a prodrug: it becomes active only when its nitro group is reduced inside anaerobic bacteria and protozoa, forming free radicals that damage DNA. That weekend she drinks wine at a party and develops flushing, throbbing headache, nausea, vomiting and palpitations.

Which explanation and additional fact about this drug are correct?
choices: An IgE reaction to the drug; it also covers MRSA well
Histamine release from fast dosing; it also treats Pneumocystis
Serotonin syndrome; it also covers vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus
A disulfiram-like reaction; it also treats C. difficile
QT prolongation; it also covers atypical respiratory pathogens

explain.html:
Motile flagellated protozoa causing vaginitis are Trichomonas, and a nitroimidazole prodrug activated by reduction in anaerobes is metronidazole. Flushing, headache, nausea and palpitations after alcohol is the disulfiram-like reaction the lecture lists for metronidazole.

Because it needs anaerobic reduction to work, metronidazole covers anaerobes (Bacteroides fragilis, Clostridium) and protozoa (Giardia, Trichomonas, Entamoeba), and the lecture lists uses including intra-abdominal infection, bacterial vaginosis, trichomoniasis and C. difficile. Its other effects are metallic taste, GI upset and peripheral neuropathy with prolonged use.
why: Alcohol-triggered flushing is not an allergy, and metronidazole does not cover aerobes such as MRSA.
Rate-related histamine release is vancomycin; Pneumocystis is treated with TMP-SMX.
Serotonin syndrome and VRE coverage describe linezolid.
Metronidazole has no atypical coverage; QT prolongation belongs to fluoroquinolones and macrolides.
explain.takeaway: Metronidazole is a prodrug reduced in anaerobes and protozoa to DNA-damaging radicals; it treats anaerobic infections, trichomoniasis and C. difficile and causes a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol.
explain.subject: Pharmacology
